passage:
Tuesday night

Today was Papa's barsi, a year since he died, and Hansa booked a dinner with her office friends for the same evening. She said she forgot. I stood in the kitchen and felt the anger come up like boiling milk. My heart was racing, my hands were shaking, and I had the perfect sentence ready: you only care about yourself, just like your mother.

It would have been true enough to hurt. That's why I wanted to say it.

I'm Jatin, and I've said things like that before and watched them sit in our marriage for months.

So I said, "I'm too angry to talk. I'm going for a walk. Twenty minutes." I walked round the colony twice. When I came back I said, "I felt forgotten today. I need you to cancel the dinner and light the lamp with me."

She cried. She cancelled it. We lit the lamp together.

qa.a: It was Papa's barsi, a year since he died.

qa.a: Jatin felt flooded with anger, with a racing heart and shaking hands, and wanted to say something deeply wounding.

qa.q: How did Jatin handle the anger wisely?
qa.a: Jatin paused, walked for twenty minutes to cool down, then spoke about the feeling of being forgotten and made a clear request.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt if Jatin had said the cruel sentence?
qa.a: Hansa would likely have felt deeply wounded and attacked, and the hurt could have stayed in the marriage for months.

grounding: The diary shows a young spouse flooded with anger who pauses, cools off and speaks about the feeling and a request instead of wounding words.

Gurpreet came home at ten and dropped her bag on the floor. I'm Yusuf, and I knew before she spoke. Her promotion dinner. I had promised to be there. I'd stayed late at the site and my phone had died.

"You weren't there," she said, voice rising. "Everyone's husband was there. I kept looking at the door."

Every part of me wanted to explain: the phone, the site, the boss. I could feel the defence ready in my mouth. And under it, fear, the cold kind: what if she's done with me?

I sat down instead. "Tell me what it was like."

She told me. It took a long time. She was angry, loud, but never frightening. If it had turned into threats, I'd have stepped away and called someone. It didn't.

When she finished, I said, "I let you down on a big night. That's on me." She sat down next to me.

qa.a: Yusuf missed Gurpreet's promotion dinner.

qa.a: Yusuf felt defensive and also afraid of losing her, with the urge to explain rushing up.

Couples counsellor's note, session 3, Arnab and Lavanya.

Lavanya arrived angry about Arnab's decision to lend their savings to his cousin without asking her. She spoke loudly and fast. Arnab's arms crossed; his foot tapped; he began, "But you don't understand, he was desperate..." I asked him to pause.

I asked Arnab what he was feeling. He said, "Scared. Like she's going to leave. So I defend."

We practised: Arnab listened for two minutes without interrupting, then said back what he heard. "You felt shut out of a decision that affects both of us." Lavanya's voice dropped. She said, "Yes. Exactly that."

Arnab then said, "I should have asked you. I'm sorry."

I also asked each of them privately whether the anger at home has ever turned into threats or intimidation. Both said no. I explained that if it ever does, staying firm and getting outside help comes first.

- Tushar

qa.a: Arnab felt scared that Lavanya might leave, and that fear made him defensive.

qa.a: Lavanya's voice dropped and she agreed, suggesting she finally felt heard.

I'm Charu, and I used to be the queen of silence. When Sunaina hurt me, forgot something important, said something careless, I'd go cold. Not a word for a day, sometimes two. I told myself I was just calming down. Really, I wanted her to suffer a little. Wanted her to guess.

Last month she missed my cousin's engagement because of a work call. I felt the familiar freeze starting. I cooked dinner in silence. She asked three times what was wrong. I said, "Nothing," and watched her face crumple.

That night I couldn't sleep. I thought about my parents, who once didn't speak for a week, and how scared I was as a child.

In the morning I said, "I'm upset about the engagement. I felt unimportant. I need a little time, and then I want to talk." Sunaina breathed out like she'd been holding her breath since yesterday.

You asked me for the podcast about the silence, so here it is. I'm Ayesha. Kishore stopped talking to me on a Sunday, after I said no to his friend staying with us for a month. Monday, nothing. Tuesday, nothing. He'd answer "hmm" and look at his phone.

I felt sick. Anxious all the time. I kept replaying everything I'd said, trying to guess my crime. I made his favourite food. I apologised for things I hadn't done. He stayed silent. I felt desperate.

On Wednesday my sister said, "You're begging. Stop. Talk to him like an adult."

So that night I sat across from him and said, calmly, "I can see you're upset. I'd really like to talk about it. But the silence is hurting me, and I think it's hurting us both. I'm not going to guess anymore."

He looked up. After a long time he said, "I felt you didn't trust my friend." And we finally talked.

At the break, Vikas came in with two cups of cutting chai from the stall outside the gate. He put one beside her. "With extra ginger. As an apology from the ginger department."

June. Dolma found out that Raghav had told his whole family about her miscarriage at a Sunday lunch, without asking her. She had wanted to tell them herself, or not at all. For a week she barely spoke to him. At night she lay awake, rehearsing all the ways she could hurt him back.

July, a Saturday. Raghav had apologised many times. That morning Dolma decided: I am going to forgive him. She told him, and felt the weight shift, a little. Only a little. "This isn't one sentence. It will take time."

August. They sat at the table and she said, calmly, "I've let go of wanting to punish you. But things need to change. Anything about my body, my health, you ask me first. Always." Raghav nodded. He wrote it on a note and stuck it on the fridge. Some mornings she still felt the old hurt. But the revenge speeches had stopped.

When I was twenty-five, your dada borrowed money from my father without telling me, and lost it in a business with his friend. My father had to sell land. I found out from my mother.

Rafael had missed Yara's father's funeral in Valencia because of a client presentation he told himself he couldn't move. He had sent flowers. For three months Yara barely looked at him.

One evening in their Madrid kitchen, she said, "I've decided to forgive you. I'm not over it. But I forgive you."

Rafael's eyes stung. Gratitude flooded him, and with it a sense of being completely undeserving. "Thank you. I don't think I've earned it."

"You haven't. That's why it's forgiveness."

He wanted to hug her, to make it all normal again. He held back. "I won't rush you."

Over the next months he kept every family date in a shared calendar. He drove her to Valencia every month to visit her mother, and sat with them, and listened to the stories about her father. He never said "I said sorry already". Yara noticed.

I'm Kiran, and here's what I used to do every time. Uday would say something like, "You were on your phone the whole dinner with my parents." And before he'd finished, I'd be talking. "I had a work message. You were on your phone last week. Why do you always attack me?" Explain, deny, blame. In about four seconds.

It felt like survival. Any criticism landed like: you are unlovable.

Last Sunday it happened again. He said I never ask about his day. I felt my mouth open, the defence ready.

I breathed instead. One long breath. Then I said, "That's true. I haven't been asking. I'm sorry." Just that.

Uday looked shocked, then his face softened. "Thank you. That's all I wanted."

Later I said, "I get defensive because criticism feels like you don't love me." He said, "It's the opposite. I say it because I want us close."

Couples counsellor's note, session 4, Saurabh and Rashmi.

Today Rashmi said, calmly, that Saurabh leaves all the planning of family events to her. Before she had finished, Saurabh was answering: "That's not true, I booked the cab for Diwali, and you never let me plan anyway, and your mother..." He spoke fast, leaning forward.

I asked him to stop and breathe. I asked what he felt when Rashmi spoke. After a pause: "Like I'm a failure. Like she's listing why I'm not good enough."

We practised again. Rashmi repeated her point. Saurabh breathed. Then he said, slowly, "Some of that's true. I leave most of it to you. I'm sorry." Rashmi's eyes filled.

Only after that did he add his side about wanting to be included in decisions. Rashmi listened properly this time.

Homework: when a complaint comes, first name one true thing in it.

- Noor

Dear Madhav bhaiya,

You asked on the phone why I sound tired. I'll write it, because saying it aloud is hard.

It's about Priyanka. For a year now, every day there's something. The way I load the dishwasher. The way I talk to her parents. The way I breathe while sleeping. Last week she said, "You're useless at everything." I've started believing I can't do anything right.

I've been trying something. When she criticises, I ask: is any of it fair? Sometimes it is. I do forget the bills. So I ask her, "What specifically would you like me to do?" That helps.

But when she says I'm useless, or a bad person, I've started saying calmly, "I won't accept that. Tell me what you need instead."

I think we need a counsellor. Could you help me find one?

Vijay

Thursday, 3 am, at my brother's flat

I found the messages tonight. Damini's phone buzzed on the sofa and I saw the name and the words and I knew. Four months. I was sick in the bathroom. My hands are still shaking. I'm Jomon, and I don't know who I am tonight. Nine years together. Was all of it fake?

My first thought was to message him, the other man. To post everything online. To tell her parents at breakfast. I had the phone in my hand.

I put it down. I don't want to do something tonight that I'll regret for years.

This isn't my failing. I keep writing that because part of me wants to find what I did wrong.

I came to my brother's. He made me tea and didn't ask questions. Tomorrow I'll call my friend Sanjay. I'm not deciding anything about the marriage this week. Maybe not this month.
